title: A serpin-myeloid axis in pancreatic cancer heterogeneity and immune evasion.
data_url: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18882157 (Xenium spatial run + imaging, CC-BY-4.0); https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE289138 (6 mouse single-cell RNA libraries)

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Read the Zenodo record (2 files, 64.6 GB total: a 45.3 GB Xenium zip and a 19.3 GB OME-TIFF image, licence CC-BY-4.0). Using HTTP range requests I read the zip's central directory (151 entries) and pulled out and parsed the small files without downloading the whole archive: cells.parquet (1,036,136 rows x 14 columns: cell_id, x/y centroid in microns, transcript_counts, areas, segmentation_method - and no biological label of any kind), features.tsv.gz (541 rows = 480 genes + 61 negative-control probes), metrics_summary.csv and experiment.xenium (1 slide, 1 region, FFPE, custom 480-gene mouse panel mMulti_480g, pixel size 0.2125 um, 1,036,136 cells), gene_panel.json (500 targets; Serpinb2, Serpine1, Spp1, Marco, Cd8a present), and analysis/clustering/gene_expression_graphclust/clusters.csv (1,032,304 rows, 31 unsupervised clusters). Separately I listed the GEO series GSE289138 file manifest (6 samples, 3 conditions x 2 chemistries, matrix.mtx.gz + barcodes + features only) and read its full series matrix metadata. I also listed the authors' GitHub repository BDBrownLab/Falcomata_PDAC_2026 (30 files, all code/notebooks, no data tables) and read its README.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The Nature article itself is paywalled (not in PubMed Central, no full text in Europe PMC), so I used the abstract plus the open bioRxiv preprint (10.1101/2025.06.11.659098) for methods and the data availability statement. From the preprint text only: the Perturb-map experiment used 35 protein barcodes in KPC mouse pancreatic tumours and analysed >4.5 million cancer and immune cells across time points; human analyses reuse public GEO GSE155698 and controlled-access HTAN dbGaP phs002371. I did not open the 19.3 GB OME-TIFF image or the 45 GB of Xenium transcript/morphology data.

a1_downloadable.note: What is deposited downloads without login: Zenodo record 18882157 under CC-BY-4.0 (I pulled real bytes by range request) and GEO GSE289138 over the open FTP/HTTPS mirror. Caveat: the paper's headline dataset - the Perturb-map multiplexed-imaging table of >4.5 million cells with their gene-knockout barcode calls - is not deposited anywhere I could find.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAIL, verified in the files. The only per-cell table released (cells.parquet) has 14 columns and every one is geometry or quality control: position, transcript counts, cell and nucleus area, segmentation method. There is no cell type, no niche label, no treatment group, no knockout assignment. Getting the paper's label (which gene was knocked out in each tumour cell) would mean downloading a 19.3 GB multiplexed immunofluorescence image, registering it to the Xenium coordinates and re-running the authors' protein-barcode deconvolution notebook. That is constructing the target, not reading it.

a3_inputs_present.note: Inputs are genuinely present: a 480-gene count matrix for 1,036,136 cells plus micron coordinates, all inside the Zenodo zip; gene identifiers are Ensembl mouse IDs with symbols.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are explicit in experiment.xenium and metrics_summary.csv: raw transcript counts per cell, coordinates and areas in microns, pixel size 0.2125 um, panel and software versions recorded.

a5_enough_rows.note: 1,036,136 cells is a big number but zero of them carry a label, and the independent experimental units are tiny: one Xenium slide/region, and six single-cell libraries covering three conditions (control, Serpinb2 knockout, Serpine1 knockout) with one library per condition per chemistry.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~1.3 GB if you take only cells.parquet (20 MB) and the 480-gene sparse matrix (~97 million non-zero entries)
a6_fits_laptop.note: The full deposit is 64.6 GB, but I demonstrated that the useful tables can be pulled out of the remote zip with range requests, so a laptop-sized working set is reachable. This is not the reason to reject.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Internally consistent where checkable: metrics_summary.csv reports 1,036,136 cells and 0.37% empty cells; the clustering file has 1,032,304 rows, a 3,832-cell difference that matches the empty-cell fraction. The preprint's >4.5 million Perturb-map cells cannot be checked because that dataset was never deposited.

a8_label_provenance.note: FAIL. The only label-shaped columns in the deposit are Xenium Ranger's own unsupervised clusters (31 graph-based clusters, plus k-means 2 to 10). Those are computed directly from the same 480-gene matrix that would be the model's input, so training on them is leakage by construction - you would be distilling the vendor's clustering, not learning biology.

existing_models.name: GITIII, a self-supervised graph transformer that infers cell-cell interactions by relating a cell's state to its surrounding neighbourhood (Nature Machine Intelligence, 2025)
existing_models.score_and_split: unknown - I saw only the search listing and did not retrieve the paper, so I will not quote a number

existing_models.name: SPACE, a cell-cell-interaction-aware cell embedding method for tissue module discovery, benchmarked on Xenium data (Cell Systems, 2024)
existing_models.score_and_split: unknown - I saw only the search listing and did not retrieve the paper

backbone.name: scGPT or Geneformer would be the natural single-cell backbones, but both expect whole-transcriptome input and this panel has only 480 genes
backbone.hardware: n/a - no label to fit a head to

integration.join_key: Ensembl mouse gene IDs are present, but genes are the features here, not the units to be joined
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Not written - without a per-cell label there is no model whose scope a join could widen.

controls.positive_control: Would have been straightforward if labels existed (recover Krt19-high tumour cells and Cd8a-high T cells from expression), but there is nothing to control.
controls.external_validation: Other public mouse pancreatic-tumour Xenium runs exist in principle, but none were checked because the project does not get that far.

honest_claim_h3: No honest claim can be made: the released files contain measurements but no measured outcome, so any 'prediction' would be of a quantity the modeller invented from the same data.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a tumour cell's 480-gene expression profile to predict which immune cells sit next to it in the tissue.
plain_idea.train_on: Single cells from a mouse pancreatic tumour measured with Xenium, an imaging method that counts individual RNA molecules in place: 1,036,136 cells, each with counts for 480 genes and an x,y position in microns. Verified by opening the files.
plain_idea.predict: The make-up of each cell's local neighbourhood - for example how many immune cells of each kind lie within 50 microns. The true answer would have to be computed by the modeller from the same expression table, because the deposit contains no cell type or neighbourhood labels.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Cancer immunologists would like to know whether a tumour cell's own gene programme forecasts the immune company it keeps, since that is the paper's central claim. But because the answer would be derived from the input data, the result would mostly measure the modeller's own definitions.

more_or_better_data.why: One Xenium slide of one mouse tumour model with a 480-gene panel. Public spatial atlases already hold many comparable runs, and this one has no annotations attached.

confidence_score.why: There is a single tissue region with no biological replicates, so there is no way to estimate how much a prediction would vary between animals or sections.

models_beatable.why: The nearby niche-modelling methods I found are from 2024-2025 and published in Cell Systems and Nature Machine Intelligence; I did not retrieve their numbers, but nothing about this unlabelled single-slide deposit suggests an edge over them.

guaranteed_improvement.why: The first condition already fails: there is no label to score anyone against, so no existing model can be run as a baseline on this data.

ml_idea: The idea that would have been attractive: take the Perturb-map experiment - 35 protein barcodes marking which gene was knocked out in each tumour cell, read out by multiplexed imaging alongside immune cell identity across more than 4.5 million cells and three time points - and learn which gene knockout a tumour cell carries from the immune neighbourhood it has built around itself. That is a real, non-circular label with a clear use. It is not reusable here because that per-cell barcode table was never deposited; the public release is one raw Xenium run, one raw image, and six raw single-cell count matrices.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed: 1,036,136 cells x 480 genes with 97 million non-zero entries is roughly 1.2 GB as a sparse float32 matrix, so a laptop could hold it. The cost is irrelevant because the labels do not exist.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Open cells.parquet and list its 14 column names - the absence of any cell type, condition or barcode column kills the project in two minutes. I did exactly this.

verdict_reason: Fails A2 and A8, verified by opening the files. The released per-cell table (1,036,136 Xenium cells) carries only coordinates, counts and areas - no cell type, no niche, no knockout assignment - so any prediction target would have to be built by the modeller, and the only label-shaped columns on offer are the vendor's own unsupervised clusters computed from the very features a model would use. The paper's actual labelled dataset, the >4.5 million Perturb-map cells with protein-barcode knockout calls, is not deposited in GEO, Zenodo or the authors' GitHub repository, which holds code only. Also fails A5 on independent units: one slide, one region, and six single-cell libraries across three conditions.
